subsection.title: Simplify Expressions with Higher Roots
subsection.p: Up to now, in this chapter we have worked with squares and square roots. We will now extend our work to include higher powers and higher roots.
Let’s review some vocabulary first.
subsection.equation: $$\begin{array}{ccl} \textbf{We write:} & & {\qquad\textbf{We say:}} \\ n^{2} & & {\qquad n\ \text{squared}} \\ n^{3} & & {\qquad n\ \text{cubed}} \\ n^{4} & & {\qquad n\ \text{to the fourth}} \\ n^{5} & & {\qquad n\ \text{to the fifth}} \end{array}$$
subsection.p: The terms ‘squared’ and ‘cubed’ come from the formulas for area of a square and volume of a cube.
It will be helpful to have a table of the powers of the integers from $$-5\ \text{to}\ 5$$. See Figure 9.4.

The second has five columns and seven rows. subsection.p: Notice the signs in Figure 9.4. All powers of positive numbers are positive, of course. But when we have a negative number, the even powers are positive and the odd powers are negative. We’ll copy the row with the powers of $$-2$$ below to help you see this.
Earlier in this chapter we defined the square root of a number.
subsection.equation: $$\text{If}\ n^{2} = m,\ \text{then}\ n\ \text{is a square root of}\ m.$$
subsection.p: And we have used the notation $$\sqrt{m}$$ to denote the principal square root. So $$\sqrt{m} \geq 0$$ always.
We will now extend the definition to higher roots.

note.p: If $$b^{n} = a$$, then $$b$$ is an nth root of a number $$a$$.
The principal nth root of $$a$$ is written $$\sqrt[n]{a}$$.
n is called the index of the radical.

subsection.p: We do not write the index for a square root. Just like we use the word ‘cubed’ for $$b^{3}$$, we use the term ‘cube root’ for $$\sqrt[3]{a}$$.
We refer to Figure 9.4 to help us find higher roots.

Could we have an even root of a negative number? No. We know that the square root of a negative number is not a real number. The same is true for any even root. Even roots of negative numbers are not real numbers. Odd roots of negative numbers are real numbers.

note.p: When $$n$$ is an even number and

list.item: $$a < 0$$, then $$\sqrt[n]{a}$$ is not a real number

note.p: When $$n$$ is an odd number, $$\sqrt[n]{a}$$ is a real number for all values of $$a$$.

subsection.p: When we worked with square roots that had variables in the radicand, we restricted the variables to non-negative values. Now we will remove this restriction.
The odd root of a number can be either positive or negative. We have seen that $$\sqrt[3]{-64} = -4$$.
But the even root of a non-negative number is always non-negative, because we take the principal nth root.
Suppose we start with $$a = -5$$.
How can we make sure the fourth root of −5 raised to the fourth power, $${(-5)}^{4}$$ is 5? We will see in the following property.

subsection.title: Use the Product Property to Simplify Expressions with Higher Roots
subsection.p: We will simplify expressions with higher roots in much the same way as we simplified expressions with square roots. An nth root is considered simplified if it has no factors of $$m^{n}$$.

note.p: $$\sqrt[n]{a}$$ is considered simplified if $$a$$ has no factors of $$m^{n}$$.

subsection.p: We will generalize the Product Property of Square Roots to include any integer root $$n \geq 2$$.

subsection.title: Add and Subtract Higher Roots
subsection.p: We can add and subtract higher roots like we added and subtracted square roots. First we provide a formal definition of like radicals.

note.p: Radicals with the same index and same radicand are called like radicals.

subsection.p: Like radicals have the same index and the same radicand.

list.item: $$5\sqrt[3]{125x}$$ and $$6\sqrt[3]{125y}$$ are not like radicals. The radicands are different.
$$2\sqrt[5]{1000q}$$ and $$-4\sqrt[4]{1000q}$$ are not like radicals. The indices are different.

subsection.p: We add and subtract like radicals in the same way we add and subtract like terms. We can add $$9\sqrt[4]{42x} + \left( {-2\sqrt[4]{42x}} \right)$$ and the result is $$7\sqrt[4]{42x}$$.

problem.p: Population growth The expression $$10 \cdot x^{n}$$ models the growth of a mold population after $$n$$ generations. There were 10 spores at the start, and each had $$x$$ offspring. So $$10 \cdot x^{5}$$ is the number of offspring at the fifth generation. At the fifth generation there were 10,240 offspring. Simplify the expression $$\sqrt[5]{\frac{10,240}{10}}$$ to determine the number of offspring of each spore.

Spread of a virus The expression $$3 \cdot x^{n}$$ models the spread of a virus after $$n$$ cycles. There were three people originally infected with the virus, and each of them infected $$x$$ people. So $$3 \cdot x^{4}$$ is the number of people infected on the fourth cycle. At the fourth cycle 1875 people were infected. Simplify the expression $$\sqrt[4]{\frac{1875}{3}}$$ to determine the number of people each person infected.
Explain how you know that $$\sqrt[5]{x^{10}} = x^{2}$$ .
Explain why $$\sqrt[4]{-64}$$ is not a real number but $$\sqrt[3]{-64}$$ is.
